claim: The PVD neuron in C. elegans has a dendritic tree composed of repetitive, stereotypical, and spatially organized structural units that resemble candelabra.
source: The dendrite morphology of the Caenorhabditis elegans' PVD bilateral neurons is composed of repetitive, stereotypical, and spatially organized structural units that resemble candelabra (Figure 1A), making it a useful platform to study dendritic morphogenesis in hermaphrodites and males (Oren-Suissa et al., 2010; Iosilevskii et al., 2024; reviewed in Heiman and Bülow, 2024).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1A showing the candelabra-like structure, as well as citations to previous work.

claim: The PVD neuron mediates response to harsh mechanical stimuli (nociception).
source: The PVD mediates several sensory modalities (reviewed in Goodman and Sengupta, 2019), notably response to harsh mechanical stimuli (nociception) (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010), response to low temperatures (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010), and proprioception (Albeg et al., 2011; Tao et al., 2019, reviewed in Krieg et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The PVD neuron mediates response to low temperatures.
source: The PVD mediates several sensory modalities (reviewed in Goodman and Sengupta, 2019), notably response to harsh mechanical stimuli (nociception) (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010), response to low temperatures (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010), and proprioception (Albeg et al., 2011; Tao et al., 2019, reviewed in Krieg et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The PVD neuron mediates proprioception.
source: The PVD mediates several sensory modalities (reviewed in Goodman and Sengupta, 2019), notably response to harsh mechanical stimuli (nociception) (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010), response to low temperatures (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010), and proprioception (Albeg et al., 2011; Tao et al., 2019, reviewed in Krieg et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PVD response to low temperatures is mediated by transient receptor potential (TRP) channels.
source: While the PVD response to low temperatures is mediated by transient receptor potential (TRP) channels (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010), nociception and proprioception are mediated by degenerins/epithelial sodium (Na+) channels (DEG/ENaCs) expressed in the PVD (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010; Husson et al., 2012), which form homo- and hetero-trimers and are involved in force sensing.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Nociception and proprioception in PVD are mediated by degenerins/epithelial sodium (Na+) channels (DEG/ENaCs).
source: While the PVD response to low temperatures is mediated by transient receptor potential (TRP) channels (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010), nociception and proprioception are mediated by degenerins/epithelial sodium (Na+) channels (DEG/ENaCs) expressed in the PVD (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010; Husson et al., 2012), which form homo- and hetero-trimers and are involved in force sensing.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: DEG/ENaCs form homo- and hetero-trimers and are involved in force sensing.
source: While the PVD response to low temperatures is mediated by transient receptor potential (TRP) channels (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010), nociception and proprioception are mediated by degenerins/epithelial sodium (Na+) channels (DEG/ENaCs) expressed in the PVD (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010; Husson et al., 2012), which form homo- and hetero-trimers and are involved in force sensing.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In mammals, some DEG/ENaCs such as ASIC1a participate in synaptic plasticity and cognitive functions such as learning and memory.
source: In mammals, some DEG/ENaCs such as ASIC1a participate in synaptic plasticity and cognitive functions such as learning and memory (Baldin et al., 2020; Bianchi and Driscoll, 2002; Chen et al., 2015; Gillespie and Walker, 2001; Gobetto et al., 2021; Hill and Ben-Shahar, 2018; Mango and Nisticò, 2020; Welsh et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Isolation of wildtype C. elegans embryos for 72 hours reduces the percentage of worms responding to harsh touch compared to crowded-raised worms.
source: We found that ~40% of isolated WT animals responded to harsh touch, compared with ~80% of animals grown in crowded plates (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: mec-4 mutants, in which gentle touch neurons are degenerated, show reduced response to harsh touch after isolation similar to wildtype animals.
source: To test whether gentle touch neurons are involved in this behavioral difference, we studied mec-4(e1611) mutants, in which gentle touch neurons are degenerated (Caneo et al., 2019; Driscoll and Chalfie, 1991; Hedgecock et al., 1983; Li et al., 2011; Suzuki et al., 2003), and obtained similar results (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 1C and citations to previous research.

claim: The isolation-induced reduction in harsh touch response is independent of gentle touch circuits.
source: Given that mec-4(e1611) exhibits the same experience-dependent behavioral plasticity as WT, we conclude that this phenomenon is independent from the mec-4 gentle touch neurons.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion based on the mec-4 mutant data.

claim: mec-3 mutants are harsh-touch-insensitive and show no response to harsh touch in both crowded and isolated conditions.
source: As a negative control, we used mec-3(e1338) mutants, that are harsh-touch-insensitive (Way and Chalfie, 1988) and found no responses for both groups (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 1C and citation to previous research.

claim: Worms grown in isolation with glass beads have a similar harsh touch response compared to animals grown in crowded plates.
source: Worms grown in isolation with beads had a similar response compared to animals grown in crowded plates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Glass beads do not fully recapitulate the crowded state for harsh touch response.
source: While the beads are sufficient to increase isolated animals' responses, they do not fully recapitulate the crowded state (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Isolation induces a reduction in harsh touch response regardless of plate 'odor' (pheromone pre-stimulation).
source: To study whether the effect was chemosensory mediated, we tested plates pre-stimulated with pheromones as well as osm-6 mutants (defective in olfactory sensory cilia; Collet et al., 1998). We found that isolation induced a reduction in the response to harsh touch, regardless of plate 'odor' (Figure 1D) or chemosensory function (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 1D and citation to previous research.

claim: Isolation induces a reduction in harsh touch response in osm-6 mutants (defective in chemosensory function).
source: To study whether the effect was chemosensory mediated, we tested plates pre-stimulated with pheromones as well as osm-6 mutants (defective in olfactory sensory cilia; Collet et al., 1998). We found that isolation induced a reduction in the response to harsh touch, regardless of plate 'odor' (Figure 1D) or chemosensory function (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and citation to previous research.

claim: Adult worms display behavioral plasticity in PVD-related harsh touch circuits that is dependent on mechanosensory experience and independent of the PDE neuron, olfactory function, and gentle touch neurons.
source: These results suggest that adult worms display a behavioral plasticity in PVD-related harsh touch circuits, which is dependent on mechanosensory experience, and is independent of the PDE neuron, olfactory function, and gentle touch neurons.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion based on the experimental results with osm-6 mutants, pheromone stimulation, and mec-4 mutants.

claim: The WT-like isolation-induced reduction in harsh touch response is present in degt-1 DEG/ENaC and gtl-1 TRP channel mutants.
source: We found that the WT-like isolation-induced reduction in harsh touch response was also present in degt-1 DEG/ENaC and gtl-1 TRP channel mutants, suggesting that these channels are not directly involved in behavioral plasticity following isolation (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: degt-1 and gtl-1 channels are not directly involved in behavioral plasticity following isolation.
source: We found that the WT-like isolation-induced reduction in harsh touch response was also present in degt-1 DEG/ENaC and gtl-1 TRP channel mutants, suggesting that these channels are not directly involved in behavioral plasticity following isolation (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as an interpretation of the data in Figure 1E.

claim: For del-1, asic-1, and mec-10 DEG/ENaC mutants, the difference in harsh touch response between isolated and crowded conditions was undetectable.
source: In contrast, for del-1, asic-1, and mec-10 DEG/ENaC mutants the difference between isolated and crowded conditions was undetectable, indicating that they are required for such behavioral plasticity.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: del-1, asic-1, and mec-10 DEG/ENaC channels are required for behavioral plasticity in response to isolation.
source: In contrast, for del-1, asic-1, and mec-10 DEG/ENaC mutants the difference between isolated and crowded conditions was undetectable, indicating that they are required for such behavioral plasticity.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The harsh touch response of asic-1 mutants was consistently high and similar to crowded WT worms, regardless of sensory experience.
source: Interestingly, while the harsh touch response of asic-1 mutants was consistently high, and similar to crowded WT worms, the response for mec-10 mutants was consistently low, similar to isolated WT animals, regardless of sensory experience (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: The harsh touch response for mec-10 mutants was consistently low, similar to isolated WT animals, regardless of sensory experience.
source: Interestingly, while the harsh touch response of asic-1 mutants was consistently high, and similar to crowded WT worms, the response for mec-10 mutants was consistently low, similar to isolated WT animals, regardless of sensory experience (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: Continuous growth in the presence of amiloride does not affect the wildtype response to harsh touch in crowded conditions.
source: We found that the response to harsh touch was not affected by continuous growth in the presence of amiloride (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Expression of MEC-10 in the PVD rescues the low response to harsh touch in crowded mec-10 mutants.
source: We found that expression of MEC-10 in the PVD rescues the low response to harsh touch in crowded mec-10 mutants, indicating that it acts cell autonomously to modulate behavioral plasticity (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 1F.

claim: MEC-10 acts cell autonomously in the PVD to modulate behavioral plasticity.
source: We found that expression of MEC-10 in the PVD rescues the low response to harsh touch in crowded mec-10 mutants, indicating that it acts cell autonomously to modulate behavioral plasticity (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as an interpretation of the rescue experiment data in Figure 1F.

claim: Isolation of crowded-raised young adults for 24 hours does not affect their response to harsh touch.
source: To determine whether isolation affects the response to harsh touch during development or in adults, we isolated crowded-raised young adults for 24 hr and found no difference in their response to harsh touch (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 1G.

claim: Isolation-induced reduction in mechanosensation is determined before early adulthood.
source: Thus, isolation-induced reduction in mechanosensation is determined before early adulthood, is PVD cell autonomous, and mec-10 dependent.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion based on the 24-hour adult isolation experiment.

claim: Isolation of embryos increases the fraction of ectopic branching in the PVD of adult worms compared to crowded age-matched worms.
source: When quantifying the branching pattern of the PVD in adulthood, WT (or WT-like him-5 background) animals which were isolated as embryos showed an increase in ectopic branching compared with crowded age-matched worms (Figure 2B)
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: Isolation of embryos causes quaternary branches of the PVD to assume a more rippled shape (fewer straight 4ry branches) compared to crowded worms.
source: When quantifying the branching pattern of the PVD in adulthood, WT (or WT-like him-5 background) animals which were isolated as embryos showed an increase in ectopic branching compared with crowded age-matched worms (Figure 2B) and the quaternary branches assumed a more rippled shape (fewer straight 4ry branches, Figure 2C), regardless of the neuron marker utilized (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chemical stimulation of plates with pheromones does not rescue the isolation-induced increase in ectopic branching or the decrease in straight quaternary branches.
source: To determine whether chemical stimulation plays a role in the observed morphological plasticity, animals were isolated onto pheromone-conditioned plates (Maures et al., 2014). Similar to the response to harsh touch (Figure 1D), chemical stimulation of the plates did not rescue the isolation-induced increase in ectopic branching or the decrease in straight quaternary branches (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and citation to previous research.

claim: Isolation of mec-4 gentle-touch-insensitive mutants causes similar changes to PVD structure as in wildtype animals.
source: Additionally, we looked at mec-4 gentle-touch-insensitive mutants (Rose et al., 2005; Suzuki et al., 2003) and found that isolation caused a similar change to PVD structure as in the WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, compare with Figure 2B, C).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and citations to previous research.

claim: Mechanosensory experience controls morphological plasticity of PVD dendritic trees independently of mec-4 and chemical stimulation.
source: In summary, these results suggest that mechanosensory experience controls morphological plasticity of PVD dendritic trees independently of mec-4 and chemical stimulation.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion based on the mec-4 mutant and pheromone stimulation experiments.

claim: Crowded mec-10 animals have more ectopic branches and fewer straight quaternary branches compared to crowded him-5 control animals.
source: We found that crowded mec-10 animals were different from WT crowded worms, and appear more isolated-like in terms of morphological features (more ectopic branches and fewer straight quaternary branches, compared to crowded him-5 control animals; Figure 2B, C).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 2B, C.

claim: PVD dendritic morphology is affected by sensory experience in a mec-10-dependent pathway.
source: These results suggest that PVD dendritic morphology is affected by sensory experience in a mec-10-dependent pathway.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as an interpretation of the mec-10 mutant morphology data.

claim: PVD-specific MEC-10 expression in crowded mec-10 mutants reduces the fraction of ectopic branches and increases the percentage of straight quaternary branches compared to non-transgenic animals.
source: To study whether mec-10 acts cell autonomously to mediate morphological plasticity, we again utilized PVD-specific MEC-10 expression in a crowded mec-10 mutant background and found it reduced the fraction of ectopic branches and increased the percentage of straight quaternary branches, compared to age-matched non-transgenic animals (Figure 2D–I).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 2D–I.

claim: MEC-10 acts in the PVD to mediate morphological plasticity.
source: Thus, MEC-10 acts in the PVD to mediate morphological plasticity.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion based on the PVD-specific rescue experiment.

claim: Isolated worms after 48 hours show a small but significant difference in the percentage of straight quaternary branches but not in ectopic branching compared to crowded worms.
source: Isolated worms showed a small but significant difference for the percentage of straight quaternary branches, but not in ectopic branching (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B–E) when compared with age-matched crowded worms, suggesting that isolation induces some morphological alterations during morphogenesis, while some relate to adult-stage maintenance of the neuron.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B–E.

claim: Isolation of young crowded adults for 24 hours induces changes in both ectopic branching and straight quaternary branches.
source: We then isolated animals grown for 48 hr in crowded conditions, and found that isolation of young crowded adults for 24 hr induced changes in both measured parameters (Figure 2—figure supplement 4F–I), recapitulating isolation of embryos (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4F–I.

claim: Isolation of adults for 24 hours is sufficient to affect PVD dendritic tree architecture.
source: Thus, isolation of adults for 24 hr is sufficient to affect PVD dendritic tree architecture, in contrast to the developmentally-established behavioral response (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion based on the 24-hour adult isolation morphology data.

claim: The presence of glass beads under isolated conditions does not reduce the fraction of ectopic branching but significantly increases the number of straight quaternary branches compared to isolated animals without beads.
source: We found that while the presence of glass beads did not reduce the fraction of ectopic branching, it significantly increased the number of straight quaternary branches (compared with isolated animals without beads, Figure 2J, K).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 2J, K.

claim: Mechanosensory stimuli from inert beads can partially rescue isolation-induced morphological changes to the PVD.
source: Thus, the mechanosensory stimuli of inert beads can partially rescue isolation-induced morphological changes to the PVD.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion based on the glass bead experiment.

claim: Isolation of adults for 2 hours has no significant consequence on the structure of the PVD.
source: We found that isolation of adults for 2 hr had no significant consequence on the structure of the PVD, while isolation of adults for 5 hr or longer significantly increased the proportion of ectopic branches and reduced the percentage of quaternary straight branches compared to crowded worms (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 3A, B.

claim: Isolation of adults for 5 hours or longer significantly increases the proportion of ectopic branches and reduces the percentage of quaternary straight branches compared to crowded worms.
source: We found that isolation of adults for 2 hr had no significant consequence on the structure of the PVD, while isolation of adults for 5 hr or longer significantly increased the proportion of ectopic branches and reduced the percentage of quaternary straight branches compared to crowded worms (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 3A, B.

claim: Isolation for 4 hours induces more growth of new branches than retraction of existing ones in the PVD.
source: This revealed isolation induced more events of ectopic branch growth and fewer events of branch retraction (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: Four hours of isolation is sufficient to induce an increase in ectopic branching and a decrease in percentage of straight quaternary branches in individual worms.
source: Furthermore, this period was sufficient to induce an increase in ectopic branching and a decrease in percentage of straight quaternary branches (Figure 3D, E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 3D, E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: During 3-hour time lapse imaging in 1% tricaine, the number of straight quaternary branches in isolated worms remains low and stable (~8%).
source: We found that while the number of straight quaternary branches in the isolated worms remained low and stable (~8%), for the crowded animals, we observed a gradual reduction in straight quaternary branches, starting after ~2 hr of isolation of individual worms on the slide (Figure 3F, G).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 3F, G.

claim: During 3-hour time lapse imaging in 1% tricaine, crowded animals show a gradual reduction in straight quaternary branches starting after ~2 hours of isolation on the slide.
source: We found that while the number of straight quaternary branches in the isolated worms remained low and stable (~8%), for the crowded animals, we observed a gradual reduction in straight quaternary branches, starting after ~2 hr of isolation of individual worms on the slide (Figure 3F, G).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 3F, G.

claim: Isolation-induced morphological plasticity is apparent within 2-3 hours from the switch from crowded conditions to growth in the absence of mechanical stimuli.
source: In summary, isolation-induced morphological plasticity is apparent within 2–3 hr from the switch from crowded conditions to growth in the absence of mechanical stimuli.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a summary conclusion based on the time course experiments.

claim: The dynamic process of isolation-induced morphological plasticity involves simultaneous increase in ectopic branching and decrease in straight terminal branches.
source: This dynamic process involves simultaneous increase in ectopic branching and decrease in straight terminal branches.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a summary of the dynamic changes observed.

claim: Blocking DEG/ENaCs by amiloride in crowded worms increases the fraction of ectopic branching and decreases the percentage of straight quaternary branches.
source: We found that blocking DEG/ENaCs by amiloride increased the fraction of ectopic branching and decreased the percentage of straight quaternary branches (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: Global inhibition of DEG/ENaCs at the sensory level alters dendritic morphology.
source: Thus, unlike harsh touch response, which is independent of sensory-level global inhibition (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), global inhibition at the sensory level alters dendritic morphology.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion based on the amiloride treatment data.

claim: Activity via degenerins modulates the structure of the PVD.
source: These results suggest that activity via degenerins modulates the structure of the PVD.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as an interpretation of the amiloride treatment results.

claim: A mixture of 0.1% tricaine and 0.01% tetramisole induces more growth than retraction of ectopic branches in crowded animals.
source: We first tested the commonly used mixture of 0.1% tricaine and 0.01% tetramisole (the racemic mixture of the enantiomer levamisole) (Kravtsov et al., 2017) and found that it induces more growth than retraction of ectopic branches in crowded animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–G).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–G and citation to previous research.

claim: 1% tricaine alone induces more retractions of ectopic branches than growth.
source: In contrast, 1% tricaine alone has the opposite effect – more retractions of ectopic branches (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H-J; Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2H-J and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: 1% tricaine induces more growth for isolated compared to crowded worms.
source: In addition, 1% tricaine induces more growth for isolated compared to crowded worms, indicating that there are activity-dependent intrinsic factors that are different for the two experience states.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data from the tricaine experiments.

claim: Modulating neuronal activity triggers structural modifications in the PVD.
source: These results suggest that modulating neuronal activity triggers structural modifications in the PVD, indicating a possible structural sensitivity to the amount of neuronal activity.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as an interpretation of the anesthetic treatment results.

claim: Mechanosensory experience, DEG/ENaC protein presence and activity, and pharmacological targeting of activity dynamically affect the structure of the PVD.
source: In summary, we found that mechanosensory experience, DEG/ENaC protein presence and activity, and pharmacological targeting of activity dynamically affect the structure of the PVD.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claim: There is no correlation between the morphology of the PVD and the response to harsh touch when testing different combinations of genotypes and treatments.
source: We found no correlation between the morphology of the PVD and the response to harsh touch when testing the different combinations of genotypes and treatments.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated based on discriminant analysis of multiple DEG/ENaC mutants.

claim: Isolated mec-10; degt-1 double mutants show crowded-like morphology with isolated-like behavioral response.
source: For example, isolated mec-10; degt-1 double mutants show crowded-like morphology with isolated-like behavioral response (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 4A and supplementary figures.

claim: Response to harsh touch is independent of the structural alteration of the PVD.
source: These findings suggest that while degenerins are required for isolation-induced plasticity of both traits, response to harsh touch is independent of the structural alteration of the PVD.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion based on the discriminant analysis and mutant data.

claim: Isolated responding and non-responding animals show no difference in the fraction of ectopic branching or the geometry of quaternary branches.
source: We then compared the dendritic morphology of responding and non-responding worms, and found that the morphological parameters were similar (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 4B–E.

claim: Analysis at the level of individual worms failed to demonstrate a correlation between the morphology and the response to harsh touch.
source: Thus, analysis at the level of individual worms failed to demonstrate a correlation between the morphology and the response to harsh touch.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion based on individual worm analysis.

claim: The morphological and behavioral phenotypes are functionally independent of each other and mediated by degenerins.
source: In summary, the morphological and behavioral phenotypes were independently affected by sensory experience via degenerins.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Worms raised in isolation are more likely to lose self-avoidance between two adjacent menorahs (candelabra).
source: In addition to the isolation-induced changes in the number of ectopic branches and the percentage of straight quaternary branches, we found that worms raised in isolation are also more likely to lose the self-avoidance between two adjacent menorahs (candelabra).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The isolation-induced loss of self-avoidance is mec-10 dependent but appears to act cell non-autonomously.
source: This effect is also mec-10 dependent, but appears to act cell non-autonomously.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated based on data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The isolation-induced loss of self-avoidance is chemosensory and amiloride independent.
source: In addition, it is chemosensory and amiloride independent (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: MEC-10 localization in the plasma membrane, intracellular vesicular compartments of the axon, and quaternary branches is reduced after isolation.
source: We found that MEC-10 localization in the plasma membrane, in intracellular vesicular compartments of the axon and in the quaternary branches was reduced after isolation (Figure 5A–D, Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 5A–D and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: DEGT-1 localization is reduced only in the cell body following isolation.
source: In contrast to MEC-10 (Figure 5A–D), DEGT-1 localization is reduced only in the cell body following isolation (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 5E–H.

claim: degt-1 mutants show reduced MEC-10 signal and abrogated the isolation-induced reduction in MEC-10 localization at the quaternary branches and the axon.
source: Furthermore, degt-1 mutants show reduced MEC-10 signal, and more importantly, abrogated the isolation-induced reduction in MEC-10 localization at the quaternary branches and the axon (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 5A–D.

claim: In mec-10 mutants, isolated worms exhibit increased DEGT-1 localization to the cell body compared with WT isolated worms.
source: In the reciprocal experiment, DEGT-1 localization was affected in mec-10 mutants, as isolated worms exhibit increased localization to the cell body compared with WT isolated worms (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 5E–H.

claim: Mechanosensory experience induces plasticity in the localization pattern of MEC-10 and DEGT-1.
source: Thus, mechanosensory experience also induces plasticity in the localization pattern of MEC-10 and DEGT-1.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion based on the localization data.

claim: Isolation significantly reduces the percentage of worms responding to optogenetic stimulation of the PVD with Channelrhodopsin.
source: We found that isolation significantly reduced the percentage of worms responding to optogenetic stimulation of the PVD (Figure 5I), indicating that the plasticity in the response is acting downstream to PVD activation, mechanosensory channels and signal transduction pathways.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 5I.

claim: The plasticity in the response to PVD activation is acting downstream to PVD activation, mechanosensory channels and signal transduction pathways.
source: We found that isolation significantly reduced the percentage of worms responding to optogenetic stimulation of the PVD (Figure 5I), indicating that the plasticity in the response is acting downstream to PVD activation, mechanosensory channels and signal transduction pathways.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as an interpretation of the optogenetic stimulation results.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of isolated animals is not sufficient to convert their dendritic trees to crowded-like morphology.
source: To determine whether optogenetic stimulation of isolated animals can reverse the morphological changes induced by the absence of mechanical stimuli in PVD, we used optogenetic stimulation of the PVD and found no significant difference between isolated and isolated optogenetically stimulated animals in any of the measured PVD structural characteristic (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reduced response of isolated animals to optogenetic stimulation suggests the escape response is not dependent on the structure of dendritic trees but on unknown downstream pathways.
source: In addition, the reduced response of isolated animals to optogenetic stimulation suggests the escape response is not dependent on the structure of dendritic trees but on unknown downstream pathways.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as an interpretation of the optogenetic stimulation results.

claim: There are no significant differences in baseline calcium levels in PVD between isolated and crowded animals.
source: To determine whether spontaneous Ca++ dynamics in PVD is different between crowded and isolated animals we first observed the baseline calcium dynamics in animals grown isolated and crowded. We found no significant differences in the calcium levels between the isolated and crowded animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both isolated and crowded animals respond similarly and efficiently to mechanical stimuli (step, sawtooth, and 10-Hz buzz) in calcium imaging experiments.
source: Using this analysis, we found that both isolated and crowded animals responded similarly and efficiently across all three types of stimuli (Figure 6, Videos 5 and 6).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 6 and Videos 5 and 6.

claim: PVD responds most strongly to a step indentation and 10-Hz buzz vibration, with a weaker response to gradual pressure 'sawtooth' stimulation.
source: Even though we observed a strong and robust activation of PVD for all three stimuli tested (Figure 6), the response to the 'sawtooth' was significantly weaker (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: PVD responds to the abrupt offset of force in the 'sawtooth' stimulation rather than the gradual onset.
source: Moreover, we noticed that the response correlated with the abrupt offset of the force in the 'saw tooth', rather than the gradual onset (Figure 6Aiii).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 6Aiii.

claim: PVD shows a separate response at both the onset and offset of a 20-second square step stimulus.
source: To corroborate this result, we also tested a 20-s square step, and indeed found a separate response at the onset as well as the offset (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Video 7).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Video 7.

claim: PVD, like TRNs, responds better to faster strain rates and adapts under continuous deformation.
source: Thus, PVD, like TRNs, responds better to faster strain rates and adapts under continuous deformation (Eastwood et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citation to previous research on TRNs.

claim: The difference in behavioral response to external mechanical stimuli is due to a pre- and/or postsynaptic effect following mechanosensory deprivation and not a direct consequence of morphological changes in the PVD or its intrinsic activity at the cell body level.
source: Together, these results suggest that the difference in the behavioral response to external mechanical stimuli is due to a pre- and/or postsynaptic effect following mechanosensory deprivation and not a direct consequence of the morphological changes in the structure of the PVD or its intrinsic activity at the level of the cell body.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion based on the calcium imaging results.

claim: Dendritic tree plasticity is independent from downstream processes that affect escape behavior in response to harsh touch.
source: In summary, our genetic and pharmacological evidence suggest that dendritic structural plasticity is an autonomous activity-dependent homeostatic mechanism. Combined with optogenetic testing and calcium imaging for mechanically stimulated PVD, our results indicate that dendritic tree plasticity is independent from downstream processes that affect escape behavior in response to harsh touch.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The sensory experience induced when one body side of the worm is in contact with the agar plate is not sufficient to maintain homeostatic dendritic structure.
source: The sensory experience induced when one body side of the worm is in contact with the agar plate is not sufficient for this purpose (Figure 7—figure supplement 1); however, other worms on the plate, or the presence of glass beads, elicit significant structural alterations.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cell autonomous activity of MEC-10 in the PVD is both necessary and sufficient to preserve the crowded-experience phenotype in terms of simplified PVD structure.
source: Moreover, the cell autonomous activity of MEC-10 in the PVD was found to be both necessary and sufficient to preserve the crowded-experience phenotype in terms of the simplified structure of the PVD.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion based on the rescue experiments.

claim: The experience-induced structural plasticity seems homeostatic at the individual branch dynamics level in the adult.
source: The experience-induced structural plasticity seems homeostatic at the individual branch dynamics level in the adult.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as an interpretation of the dynamic imaging results.

claim: The behavioral response to harsh touch is modulated by mechanosensory experience during development and by the presence of DEG/ENaCs.
source: In contrast, we show that the behavioral response to harsh touch is modulated by mechanosensory experience during development and by the presence of DEG/ENaCs, and perhaps involves other neurons downstream.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion based on the developmental timing and genetic experiments.

claim: The behavioral plasticity is a pre- and/or postsynaptic property mediated by DEG/ENaCs and related to neurotransmission modulation, independently of the structure of the PVD dendritic tree.
source: Based on optogenetic stimulation, we presume that the behavioral plasticity is a pre- and/or postsynaptic property, mediated by DEG/ENaCs (Hill and Ben-Shahar, 2018) and related to neurotransmission modulation, independently of the structure of the PVD dendritic tree.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as an interpretation based on optogenetic stimulation results and citation to previous research.

claim: The structural and behavioral plasticity are separated in time (adulthood vs. development) and space (dendrite vs. axon).
source: These structural and behavioral plasticity are separated in time (adulthood vs. development) and space (dendrite vs. axon; Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and illustrated in Figure 7.
